catalog_locator: Part II 'The languages of the Gunggari group', Phonetic notes, section 2.11, p.178. Cross-refs: Part I 2.9, p.5; Part I consonant-letter key, p.4; Bidjara 8.5, pp.204-205 (the stress sentence runs across the page break onto p.205).
catalog_quote: 2.11 Word or syllable stress is not significant in any of the languages studied here. The spoken context runs smooth without emphasis of any syllable unless in cases of long vowels (or diphthongs), besides not very frequent in the Gunggari languages. As usual, in a spoken context or sequence of syllables, however, the second initial syllable often carries mechanically more stress than the others (cf. in Part I, 2.9), which explains the origin of such shortened forms as ɗe· (Gun EA) for jinɗia where?; this tendency is frequently reflected in the current pronunciation of place names of several syllables, derived from Aboriginal words, in Queensland: Barálba, Mundúbbera etc. In consequence of the above remarks, the separation of words or flectional elements (that is lexical or morphological units) must be made chiefly on the basis of etymology and must, in some cases, be arbitrary ...

new_statements.rule_in_words: Holmer: stress is non-contrastive and no syllable is perceptibly emphasized in Gunggari (and the other Maric languages he recorded), apart from prominence on long vowels; in connected speech or longer words there is a non-distinctive tendency for the second syllable to be somewhat stronger (illustrated by Gunggari jingia > ge· 'where?').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing for Gunggari. (For Bidjara, same volume 8.5 pp.204-205, Holmer mentions secondary stress on alternate syllables after a second-syllable accent; Breen 1981 for Margany/Gunya gives secondary stress on the 3rd syllable of 4-syllable words under initial main stress.)
new_statements.exceptions: Long vowels or diphthongs attract emphasis; second-syllable prominence is described as a tendency of connected speech/long words, not a rule; word division must therefore be made on etymological grounds.
new_statements.domain_note: Group-level statement for all 'Gunggari group' (Maric) languages in the survey, with a Gunggari example; refers to 'spoken context or sequence of syllables' (utterance level) rather than citation forms. Conflicts with Breen's first-hand initial-stress descriptions of sister dialects Margany/Gunya (1981) and Bidyara (1973); Holmer makes the identical 'not significant, second syllable tendency' claim for every language in the survey (Wakka group, Manandjali 9.6, Darumbal), so it may reflect his transcription practice more than Gunggari prosody.
new_statements.identity_note: Holmer's 'Gunggari' is the 'Roma language' associated with Roma, Mitchell and the Maranoa River (Part II 1.3 p.175, 4.1 p.179), i.e. Southern Maric Gunggari = kung1258 / AIATSIS D37. It is NOT the Barcoo-River Kuungkari (Glottolog kuun1236, Breen 1990 PL B-105), even though Glottolog's coordinates for kung1258 (-24.2, 143.2) sit in Kuungkari country. Holmer's stress paragraph (2.11) is a group-level statement for all the 'Gunggari group' (= Mari/Maric) languages he studied (Gunggari, Bidjara, Marganj, Gangulu, Wirri, Birri, Ngawun), illustrated with a Gunggari example; his main Gunggari informant (Gun TC) was an L2-fluent speaker born at Angledool NSW, others from Roma/Mitchell/St George/Bendena. Note the conflict with Breen 1981 (HAL 2:295) who reports regular initial main stress for the sister dialects Margany and Gunya, and with Breen 1973 for Bidyara (initial stress, per Hayes 1995); Holmer's 'not significant / second syllable mechanically stronger' claim is one he repeats for every Queensland language in the survey.

sources.note: Part II ('The languages of the Gunggari group') phonetic notes 2.11, p.178: word/syllable stress 'not significant' in any of the Gunggari-group languages; speech runs without emphasis on any syllable except long vowels; in connected speech the second syllable often carries mechanically more stress (Gunggari example ge. < jingia 'where?'). The Gunggari chapter itself (5.1-5.10, pp.181-184) adds nothing on stress; Part I 2.9 p.5 states the same survey-wide.
